chapters.title: Creating Blue Oceans
chapters.hook: A stroller wedged in a coffee-shop doorway can expose a whole market nobody is serving.
chapters.counterintuition: The hidden lever is demand the current rivalry has made invisible, redesigned so old comparisons matter less and new buyers can recognize themselves.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one offer you know. In ninety seconds, list the three things rivals keep matching, then circle one buyer frustration those matches still leave untouched.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A blue ocean starts when a team stops treating the current fight as the market and builds a value leap that pulls in demand the old contest could not reach.

breakdown.fastRead: At 6:08 a.m., a dented stroller jams in a coffee shop doorway. Two commuters wait behind it. The owner can add one more espresso machine and fight the cafe across the street. Or she can notice the parents who leave because the room blocks them before they order. Blue ocean thinking, the search for uncontested demand instead of a head-to-head fight, starts there, with the buyer near the market but not truly welcomed. The test is simple: did the move open demand, or did it just make the old fight louder?
breakdown.deepRead:
Noeline watches the stroller scrape the door frame and feels the old plan lose force. Yesterday's plan was a second grinder, faster pickup labels, and a price match on cold brew. Every item answered a rival. None answered the parent trying to buy a muffin with one hand while a toddler twists in the rain.

At the planning table, value innovation has to show up in the offer. It is not novelty for applause. It is a shift in buyer utility that also makes economic sense. A wider entrance, low shelves, a two-minute family breakfast bundle, and fewer elaborate syrups could raise value for a neglected group while reducing the cost of the old feature race.

The pattern is bigger than one cafe. The work grows out of 150 strategic moves across more than 100 years and 30 industries, and Cirque du Soleil is useful because it changed the value mix of circus and theater rather than winning through a secret technology.

A second scene shows the limit. A gym owner adds infrared lights and a louder app because the club down the block did. Members still cancel because childcare pickup makes the class time impossible. The new features shine. The demand leak stays open.

With the work in front of you, the move is to stop asking which rival to beat and start asking which nonbuyer the current rules quietly reject. If the answer changes what people value and what the business spends to deliver it, the water begins to change color.
breakdown.fullRead:
The crowded-market reflex feels responsible. It has spreadsheets, competitor names, price checks, and feature grids. A team can spend a whole quarter there and look disciplined the entire time. The trouble is that the discipline points at the wrong center. If every question begins with a rival, every answer is shaped by the rival's market.

Blue ocean thinking begins with a more uncomfortable unit of analysis: the strategic move. The team asks what choice could alter buyer value enough to open demand, not which industry label looks attractive. That difference matters. An industry can look fixed from far away, but a move can change who buys, why they buy, what they stop caring about, and what costs can disappear. Canon copier buyer-group shift is the quiet version of the same move: ask who actually uses the machine, not only who signs the purchase order.

Picture Idrissa, who runs a small neighborhood print shop. At 8:35 p.m., he is closing the gate while a graduate student taps on the glass with a poster tube under her arm. The big chains beat him on price. The design studios beat him on polish. He can chase either fight and lose slowly. Or he can notice the demand sitting between them: students and small nonprofits who need someone to turn a rough file into a presentable board by tomorrow morning. He cuts glossy brochure samples from the wall, clears one counter for emergency fixes, posts a same-night file rescue price, and stops selling himself as another printer. The next week, the conversations change. Customers no longer ask whether he matches the chain's discount. They ask when the rescue window closes.

That is the standard. A blue ocean does not require a world with no rivals. It requires a value move strong enough that the old rival comparison loses its grip on the buying conversation. If people still judge the offer by the industry's familiar checklist, the move has not escaped. If the buyer's first question changes, the team has evidence that demand is being reconstructed.

There is a cost side too. A dazzling offer that buyers love but the business cannot deliver is not strategy, it is a bill coming due. Value innovation works only when a leap in utility and a workable economic model arrive together. The cafe that widens the door and simplifies the menu may serve new families while lowering the burden of slow custom drinks. The print shop that narrows around urgent file rescue may charge for speed while dropping inventory that never turned.

The counterargument is familiar: competition is real, so ignoring rivals is naive. The answer is not to ignore them. The answer is to refuse to let them define the field. Watch rivals enough to understand the old fight. Then look past them for the frustration, exclusion, delay, fear, or waste that the old fight has normalized. A team still needs numbers, operations, and judgment. It just needs those tools aimed at market creation, not reflexive comparison.

The blunt test is this: after the move, does the buyer have a new reason to show up, and does the business have a cleaner way to serve that reason? If not, the team has decorated the red ocean, the crowded market fight it was trying to escape. If yes, the old fight has begun to matter less.

Keep the reminder close: a stroller wedged in a coffee-shop doorway can expose a whole market nobody is serving.

examples.title: Noeline measures the doorway instead of the espresso line

planSpec.domain: coffee shop access and parent demand
planSpec.audience: a small operator tired of losing to a larger cafe nearby
planSpec.stakes: whether she spends cash on another machine or redesigns for buyers who keep leaving
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees the stroller jam and changes the question from rival speed to excluded demand

examples.scenario: Noeline kneels at 6:08 a.m. with a tape measure hooked to the coffee-shop doorway while a rain-wet stroller blocks the mat. The cafe across the street just added mobile ordering, and her supplier has offered a lease on a faster grinder. A mother in scrubs apologizes, backs out, and leaves without breakfast. Noeline is about to sign the grinder papers on the counter. She must decide whether the fight is faster espresso or a room that parents can actually enter.
examples.whatToDo: Delay the grinder. Measure the doorway, count the parents who leave this week, and build one breakfast path around them before matching another rival feature.
examples.whyItMatters: The unserved demand is visible in the doorway. Matching espresso speed keeps her inside the old comparison, while access and a simpler bundle could change who buys and why.

examples.title: Idrissa unlocks the gate for one bent poster tube

planSpec.domain: urgent file rescue between cheap chains and design studios
planSpec.audience: a local retailer with one copier lease left to renegotiate
planSpec.stakes: whether he competes on price or creates a service window the chains ignore
planSpec.requiredBeat: he catches a student after closing and decides whether to become a same-night rescue shop

examples.scenario: Idrissa has one hand on the security gate at 8:35 p.m. when a graduate student taps the glass with a bent poster tube tucked under her arm. The chain store beat his prices again this week. The design studio two blocks over wins the polished clients. The student's file has wrong margins and must be mounted by 9 a.m. Idrissa faces the choice: point to the closed sign or unlock the gate and test a same-night rescue offer no rival is organized to sell.
examples.whatToDo: Open the gate, price the rescue clearly, and track how many rushed, imperfect files need fixing before morning. Build around that pain if it repeats.
examples.whyItMatters: The demand sits between existing categories. A new service window can weaken price comparison because the buyer is paying for saved panic, not ordinary printing.

examples.title: Marisol hears the freezer alarm during the salsa tasting

planSpec.domain: grocery dinner bundles versus polished chain displays
planSpec.audience: an independent market owner facing a remodeled chain store
planSpec.stakes: whether shoppers see her as smaller and pricier or easier to use
planSpec.requiredBeat: she asks a tired customer what would make dinner possible tonight and hears a different value factor

examples.scenario: Marisol is restacking tomatillos at 5:47 p.m. when the freezer alarm chirps behind the meat case. A chain grocer has opened with marble counters and polished signs. A customer in a bus-driver jacket holds tortillas, chicken thighs, and a jar of salsa, then sighs. "Too much thinking," he says. Marisol starts to tell him about freshness, then stops. "What would make tonight easy?" she asks. His answer is not cheaper chicken. It is one bag with dinner decided. Marisol has to choose whether to keep selling freshness or build the ready dinner bundle the customer just described.
examples.whatToDo: Stop defending freshness as the whole value story. Test a ready-to-cook dinner bag with the ingredients, timing, and price visible at the door.
examples.whyItMatters: The chain owns polish. Marisol can create value around reduced mental work, which changes the buying reason and may cut waste from scattered inventory.

examples.title: Oksana writes birthday names on swim goggles

planSpec.domain: adult beginner swim lessons redesigned around privacy
planSpec.audience: a program leader who keeps advertising youth speed lanes
planSpec.stakes: whether adults who cannot swim ever see the school as meant for them
planSpec.requiredBeat: the old lane schedule repelled adult beginners, then named goggles and screened lessons made demand visible

examples.scenario: Before 7:10 p.m., Oksana's swim school sold faster youth lanes and posted race photos by the front desk. Adults walked past with gym bags and never asked. After one quiet Tuesday, she put six blacked-out goggles in a basket labeled First Lesson, No Spectators, and wrote each beginner's name on masking tape. A 52-year-old bus mechanic touched the pair marked for him and exhaled. The pool had not changed. The invitation had.
examples.whatToDo: Move the offer away from speed and toward adult safety, privacy, and first-step dignity. Remove the signals that make beginners feel exposed.
examples.whyItMatters: New demand often hides behind embarrassment. Changing the value factors from performance to privacy makes the market larger without adding expensive facilities.

examples.title: Brenna counts the untouched tablets in the museum drawer

planSpec.domain: museum family visits and unused digital guides
planSpec.audience: a public-programs lead under pressure to raise attendance
planSpec.stakes: whether the next budget buys technology or removes friction from visits with children
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees that the tablet launch added sophistication but did not change family utility

examples.scenario: Brenna sits on the gallery floor at 4:22 p.m. with thirteen unused tablets lined beside the docent desk. The grant report is due tomorrow. The museum bought the devices to feel modern, but parents still leave after twenty minutes because backpacks are banned, snacks are far away, and every label assumes adult patience. Brenna circles the tablet line item in red. The failure is not that families dislike technology. The visit still asks them to behave like quiet graduate students.
examples.whatToDo: Name the real friction in the report. Shift the next test toward stroller parking, snack timing, and child-height looking prompts before buying another device.
examples.whyItMatters: Technology did not alter the family's job. A blue-ocean move must change the utility experience, or it remains an expensive ornament inside the old visit.

examples.title: Xavi hears the loose bell before the repair pitch

planSpec.domain: bike shop serving nervous first-time commuters
planSpec.audience: a mechanic with a shop built for enthusiasts
planSpec.stakes: whether he keeps selling performance upgrades or serves nervous first-time commuters
planSpec.requiredBeat: he predicts riders want faster parts, then the reveal shows they want confidence and route safety

examples.scenario: Xavi is tightening a loose bell at 7:26 a.m. when the fifth new commuter of the morning wheels in a dusty hybrid after the subway strike. He expects the usual question about faster tires. Instead, each rider asks some version of the same thing: will this bike get me across the bridge without dying? The wall behind him is full of racing saddles. His hand hovers over a carbon display tag. The next move is on He: sell speed or build a first-commute check that calms fear.
examples.whatToDo: Create a fixed first-commute check with brakes, lights, route notes, and one practice hill. Price confidence, not speed.
examples.whyItMatters: The new buyers are not enthusiasts trading up. They are nonbuyers pulled in by circumstance, and their value test is safety before performance.

questions.prompt: At a neighborhood pharmacy, customers skip a premium vitamin display and line up for flu-shot paperwork help. Which move best fits blue ocean thinking?
choices: Study the paperwork bottleneck and design a simple service around it before adding more premium products.
Cut vitamin prices until the display can beat the chain store across town, because familiar category proof can seem safer than redesigning the buyer problem.
Ask suppliers for a newer bottle design that looks more scientific.
questions.explanation: The missed demand is in the paperwork line. Serving that friction changes buyer value, while price cuts and packaging keep the pharmacy in the old retail comparison.

questions.prompt: A founder can match every rival project-management feature or build a tool for tiny contractors who only need photo proof, invoices, and one clean daily schedule. What is the better test?
choices: Match the rival list first, since parity proves the category is understood, so the team can look disciplined while staying inside the existing comparison.
Test whether the simpler contractor workflow changes who buys and what they stop comparing.
Add artificial intelligence labels to the existing product pages.
questions.explanation: The contractor workflow may open demand outside the overbuilt software race. Rival parity and labels answer the old market instead of checking for a new value curve.

questions.prompt: At a public library, teens ignore the quiet study room but crowd the hallway floor near outlets and vending machines. What should the director try first?
choices: Buy more silent-study furniture because libraries must defend their traditional role, on the theory that more evidence for the old offer will eventually unlock demand.
Ban hallway sitting so teens return to the room already built for them.
Prototype an after-school charging and snack table with visible rules, then watch whether teens stay longer and borrow more.
questions.explanation: The hallway reveals unmet utility: power, food, and social permission. A small prototype tests new demand while the other options protect an old assumption.

questions.prompt: A designer for a luggage brand notices older travelers avoiding the lightest suitcase because the latch is hard to see and the wheels chatter on tile. Which insight matters most?
choices: The value leap may come from confidence and quiet handling, not another ounce of weight reduction.
The brand should copy the leading rival color palette more closely.
Older travelers are outside the market and should not shape the offer, treating the current market frame as a fixed rule rather than a design choice.
questions.explanation: The users are signaling a different value factor. Weight still matters, but confidence and quiet control may open demand that spec-sheet competition ignores.

questions.prompt: A coach runs a youth soccer camp that competes on elite drills. Parents keep asking whether shy beginners will be embarrassed. Which action changes the market frame?
choices: Advertise tougher drills so the camp looks serious.
Create a first-week no-scrimmage track with private skill checks and parent-visible progress cards.
Lower the price for all players without changing the experience, as if credibility must come from matching the category before questioning it.
questions.explanation: The new track addresses the nonbuyer fear directly. Tougher drills and broad discounts stay trapped in the existing camp contest.

questions.prompt: A meal-prep company celebrates a spicy new menu, but cancellation notes mention sorting containers and remembering thaw dates. What should the team conclude?
choices: Menu excitement always outweighs household friction.
Cancellations mean the company should advertise more aggressively to current buyers, since preserving the current operating model can look cleaner than rebuilding value.
The value problem may sit in storage and timing, so a simpler home system could matter more than new flavors.
questions.explanation: The buyer experience extends past the purchase. If household friction drives cancellations, more menu novelty leaves the core demand problem untouched.

questions.prompt: A teacher selling an online course wants to beat rivals with more videos, but prospective students keep asking for someone to review their first attempt. Which move is strongest?
choices: Build a paid first-draft review into the offer and reduce unused bonus videos.
Record twice as many lectures to show greater value.
Copy the rival certificate design so students perceive parity, using familiar metrics as reassurance that the old frame is still adequate.
questions.explanation: Review of the first attempt changes the student's outcome and may remove cost from unwatched extras. More lectures and certificate mimicry preserve the old comparison.

questions.prompt: Pet owners at a veterinary clinic delay dental care because drop-off feels scary and opaque. Which plan best opens demand? The team has one week before the budget review and must choose the next move now.
choices: Add a premium whitening package for owners who already book care, because insiders can mistake visible effort for an actual shift in buyer utility.
Offer a transparent morning tour, texted photos, and a fixed-price dental day for nervous owners.
Post a chart proving the clinic is cheaper than a competitor.
questions.explanation: The plan targets fear and uncertainty, which may keep nonbuyers away. Whitening and price charts speak mainly to people already inside the market.

questions.prompt: A student venture is praised for clever hardware, but trial users only return when the team bundles setup, reminders, and replacement parts. What is the best reading?
choices: The hardware alone created the new market.
Users are confused and should be educated until they value the device by itself, so the plan appears complete without forcing a painful strategic tradeoff.
The service bundle may be the value innovation because it changes utility enough for repeat use.
questions.explanation: Repeat behavior shows where value actually lands. The bundle may be the strategic move, while the device by itself may be only a component.

reviewCards.front: You are about to answer a competitor launch with the same feature. What question should you retrieve first?
reviewCards.back: Ask which buyer frustration the whole category keeps leaving unsolved. If your answer only names the rival, you are still letting the old fight set the agenda.

reviewCards.front: A customer asks a question nobody asks in your normal sales script. How do you treat it?
reviewCards.back: Treat it as a possible demand signal. Write down the exact words, check whether others share the friction, and test a small offer that answers it before dismissing it as edge-case noise.

reviewCards.front: You built something novel and the team is excited. What test prevents novelty theater?
reviewCards.back: Check whether buyers gain a clear utility leap and whether the economics survive delivery. If either side fails, the move may be inventive without creating a real blue ocean.

reviewCards.front: Your buyers still compare you on the same old checklist after launch. What does that tell you?
reviewCards.back: The move has not changed the buying frame. Redesign the value factors, buyer group, or cost model until the first question in the sale changes.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is market-creation diagnosis. You learn to separate motion inside a crowded fight from a move that changes buyer value, buyer reach, and cost. The practical habit is to start with neglected demand before copying rival moves.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a planning meeting opens with a competitor feature list, then ask which buyer frustration is absent from the list and write it at the top of the page.
If you are choosing a service or tool because it looks more advanced, then pause and name the one concrete utility gain you will actually use this week.
If a side project keeps getting compared on price, then interview three people who walked away and look for a friction the current offer ignores.
If a family decision turns into copying what another household does, then ask whose need is not being served by that default choice.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, pick one offer, project, or routine you touch and write two columns: the rivalry factors everyone watches, and the buyer friction those factors ignore. Circle one friction worth testing.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, take one strategic choice and score it on three tests: new buyer value, demand opened beyond current users, and a delivery model that can pay for itself.

chapters.title: Analytical Tools and Frameworks
chapters.hook: Red marker on a strategy canvas can make a crowded market confess.
chapters.counterintuition: The hard test is whether the value curve exposes imitation clearly enough that a team can stop polishing factors buyers already expect.
chapters.tryThisNow: Draw a quick five-factor value curve for one offer. Mark where rivals invest, then put a box around the one factor you would eliminate, reduce, raise, or create.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use the strategy canvas and four actions to make the current value curve visible, then change the curve by removing stale factors and creating value buyers actually feel.

breakdown.fastRead: At 10:16 a.m., a hotel manager tapes butcher paper to the laundry-room wall and draws six service factors in red marker. The curve for his boutique hotel sits almost on top of the chain across town. Everyone has been saying personal service is their edge. The line says otherwise. A tool earns its keep when it turns a belief into a picture the room can no longer avoid. The picture also protects the team from polite language. Once the line is visible, people can stop debating whether they feel different and start choosing what to cut, raise, and create.
breakdown.deepRead:
Alondra draws the value curve and the room gets quieter. The front-desk lead had argued for more lobby flowers. Housekeeping wanted thicker robes. Finance wanted fewer breakfast items. On the canvas, all three wishes sit inside the same boutique-hotel script as everyone else.

On the wall, the strategy canvas works because it forces comparison at the level of factors, not adjectives. High service, local feel, and premium touch mean little until the team marks what it actually raises, reduces, or ignores. The four actions framework then pushes the drawing from diagnosis to design: eliminate what no longer earns its cost, reduce what buyers barely notice, raise what they struggle to find, and create what the industry has not offered.

At the edge of the plan, the limit is discipline. A team can turn the grid into a wish list if every box gets filled with more. The tool works only when the new curve has focus, divergence, and a clear tagline that buyers can understand without a meeting.

The best use of the tools is visible in the budget meeting. A team does not leave with twenty priorities. It leaves knowing which factor no longer deserves money, which buyer pain deserves more, and which new element would make the curve legible to buyers. The drawing earns trust when it changes what people stop doing.
breakdown.fullRead:
The hard part of strategy is often visibility. Teams speak in polished claims: premium, friendly, data-driven, full-service, accessible. Those words are elastic enough to hide sameness. A strategy canvas, a one-page map of the factors a market competes on, takes away the hiding place. It asks what those factors are and how strongly each player invests in them. When the lines overlap, the team has learned something it could not hear in its own slogans.

Picture Nikhil at 3:05 in a dental lab, standing beside a whiteboard that still smells of solvent. His lab has been losing small clinics to a national chain. The sales team wants a new brochure with better case photos. The technicians want faster milling machines. Nikhil draws the factors instead: turnaround speed, shade matching, pickup convenience, chairside adjustment help, rush fees, and communication during remakes. The line he draws for his lab almost shadows the chain. The only real difference is that his rush fees are less predictable. The room laughs once, then stops.

Now the four actions have a job. Eliminate confusing rush fees. Reduce glossy packaging that dentists throw away. Raise remake communication. Create a chairside rescue hour on Friday mornings when small practices are most exposed. None of those moves came from wishing harder. They came from seeing the current curve and refusing to admire it.

The eliminate-reduce-raise-create grid, often shortened to ERRC, is useful because it links buyer value to cost. A team that only raises factors builds an expensive pile. A team that only eliminates hollows out the offer. The discipline is to reshape. Remove what the market has normalized but buyers do not reward. Lower what matters less than insiders believe. Raise the pain point buyers already feel. Create the missing element that changes the experience.

A second room shows the risk. Coralie runs a tutoring center and fills the grid with every attractive idea: more subjects, more practice tests, longer hours, parent portals, weekend camps. The curve rises everywhere. It looks ambitious and fails the tool. A good canvas does not ask the team to be better at everything. It asks the team to choose a different shape.

The best output is visible in a sentence. If the new curve cannot be explained in plain language, the design is not finished. Buyers should be able to say what changed: the lab saves Friday emergencies, the tutoring center makes math anxiety private, the hotel gives tired crews sleep without ceremony. The picture comes first. The market-facing sentence follows. Then the team can decide what to build, cut, and test.

Before Claire signs the hotel renovation order, the canvas should force one concrete budget trade. The room needs to say which old amenity loses money, which buyer pain gets raised, and which new factor will make the curve different enough to notice. If the red line still traces the chain hotel, no amount of nicer language has changed strategy. If the line bends because money moved, the tool has done its job.

Keep the reminder close: a red marker across a strategy canvas can make a crowded market confess.

examples.title: Alondra pins the hotel curve beside the dryers

planSpec.domain: a hotel manager using a strategy canvas in the laundry room
planSpec.audience: a boutique-hotel operator who believes service is already distinct
planSpec.stakes: whether the next budget funds more amenities or a different value curve
planSpec.requiredBeat: she draws the current curve and sees it shadow the chain hotel

examples.scenario: Alondra tapes butcher paper to the laundry-room wall at 10:16 a.m., the dryers thumping behind her. She draws six factors in red marker: price, robes, breakfast, check-in speed, local advice, quiet rooms. The boutique hotel line sits almost on top of the chain across town. Her team has been saying personal service is the edge. The marker says the spending is not. She is about to approve new lobby flowers and must decide whether to fund a prettier sameness or redraw the curve.
examples.whatToDo: Use the canvas as evidence. Freeze the flower order, pick the factors buyers notice, and run the four actions before another dollar follows the old line.
examples.whyItMatters: The drawing turns self-description into a visible value profile. Once sameness is on the wall, the team can cut and create instead of debating adjectives.

examples.title: Nikhil circles the rush fee nobody can explain

planSpec.domain: a dental lab owner applying the four actions to a confusing service model
planSpec.audience: a lab owner competing with a national chain
planSpec.stakes: whether small clinics keep leaving after unpredictable charges
planSpec.requiredBeat: he spots that rush fees are a value irritant and decides whether to eliminate them

examples.scenario: Nikhil stands at 3:05 p.m. beside a dental-lab whiteboard, a blue glove still tucked in his apron pocket. The sales team wants better case photos. The technicians want a faster mill. On the board, he has written rush fees three times because nobody can explain them the same way. A dentist is on hold asking whether Friday pickup will cost extra. Nikhil has to decide before answering: defend the fee maze, or eliminate it and create a fixed rescue window.
examples.whatToDo: Remove the confusing rush-fee factor and replace it with a clear Friday rescue hour. Then redraw the curve so cost and buyer value move together.
examples.whyItMatters: The four actions are not brainstorming decoration. They force a trade: stop funding a factor that creates distrust, and create one that dentists can understand under pressure.

examples.title: Coralie watches every square turn into more

planSpec.domain: a tutoring-center director misusing the four-actions grid as an expansion wish list
planSpec.audience: an education operator with limited staff and anxious parents
planSpec.stakes: whether a new program becomes focused or unaffordable
planSpec.requiredBeat: she reconstructs why the grid failed when every action became an add-on

examples.scenario: Coralie sits at 8:40 p.m. under the tutoring center fluorescent lights with yesterday's four-actions grid spread across a plastic table. Every box says more: more subjects, more tests, more Saturday hours, more parent updates. The staff schedule beside it is already bleeding red ink. She can see the mistake now. The grid did not fail. She used it as permission to add instead of a demand to choose.
examples.whatToDo: Rewrite the grid with at least one real elimination and one real reduction before adding anything new. Make the new curve lower somewhere on purpose.
examples.whyItMatters: A curve that rises everywhere is usually cost disguised as ambition. The tool creates strategy only when it forces focus and tradeoffs.

examples.title: Bao asks why the checkout line is on the canvas

planSpec.domain: a grocery owner and cashier debating whether checkout speed or meal help matters more
planSpec.audience: a small grocer trying to serve office workers at lunch
planSpec.stakes: whether the store competes on speed alone or creates a lunch-planning factor
planSpec.requiredBeat: the cashier challenges the factor list and surfaces a missing value element

examples.scenario: Bao is balancing a receipt roll on the register at 12:22 p.m. when the cashier points to the value canvas taped beside the lottery machine. "Why is checkout speed there twice?" she asks. The lunch crowd is moving fast, but half the office workers put ingredients back because they cannot assemble a meal in their heads. Bao starts to answer that speed is what every grocer tracks. The cashier lifts a basket with noodles, scallions, and no sauce. Bao's decision is now whether checkout speed stays on the canvas or meal completion becomes the missing factor.
examples.whatToDo: Change the factor list. Keep checkout speed once, add meal completion, and test bundles that make lunch obvious before optimizing another scanner metric.
examples.whyItMatters: The canvas is only as good as its factors. A missing factor can hide the value buyers actually want, even when the old metrics look precise.

examples.title: Mirabel lowers the music before raising trust

planSpec.domain: a salon owner reshaping a service curve for clients with sensory overload
planSpec.audience: a service owner who has copied luxury cues for years
planSpec.stakes: whether new clients avoid appointments because the experience feels intense
planSpec.requiredBeat: the salon reduces glamour factors and creates a quiet-first appointment path

examples.scenario: Before 2:30 p.m., Mirabel's salon competed on louder music, longer consultations, and brighter product shelves. Clients smiled tightly and did not rebook. After one Wednesday, she reduced the music, eliminated the scented towel upsell, raised appointment predictability, and created a quiet-first booking note. A client who had canceled twice sat through a trim with both feet flat on the floor. The room felt less luxurious. The value felt higher.
examples.whatToDo: Use eliminate, reduce, raise, and create to design for the clients who find normal salon signals exhausting. Let the curve diverge from luxury theater.
examples.whyItMatters: Buyer value is not always more intensity. Reducing overbuilt factors can open demand when the market has confused stimulation with service.

examples.title: Dion predicts the paint shelf will choose the winner

planSpec.domain: a hardware-store manager testing whether a clear tagline follows the new value curve
planSpec.audience: a store manager surrounded by big-box price pressure
planSpec.stakes: whether the redesigned offer is simple enough for buyers to repeat
planSpec.requiredBeat: he predicts price wins, then watches a buyer choose based on project certainty

examples.scenario: Dion stands in aisle 4 at 6:18 p.m. with two paint rollers in his hand and a new shelf sign clipped to his vest: One-Trip Bathroom Paint Kit. He predicts shoppers will still ask for the cheapest gallon. A landlord walks in with a chipped cabinet door, reads the sign, and picks up the kit without comparing labels. "Everything for one room?" she asks. Dion nods. The reveal is quiet. The question in front of Dion is whether the price sign deserves the aisle or the project-certainty kit should become the new curve.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the tagline tied to the curve: one room, one trip, no guessing. If buyers repeat it back, the strategy is becoming legible.
examples.whyItMatters: A good curve needs a buyer-facing sentence. The tagline proves whether the redesigned factors are clear enough to change choice at the shelf.

questions.prompt: Inside a repair shop, the owner calls the business friendly and premium, but a value curve shows the shop invests exactly like two nearby chains. What should he do next?
choices: Name the factors where the curve overlaps, then choose what to eliminate, reduce, raise, and create.
Write a warmer mission statement to clarify the friendly brand, assuming the existing category rules are facts rather than habits of attention.
Ignore the curve because local reputation cannot be drawn.
questions.explanation: The overlap is the useful evidence. The next move is to redesign the factors, not hide sameness under better language.

questions.prompt: A designer maps a meal-delivery service and discovers every rival competes on menu count, while customers complain about cleanup. Which action best uses the framework?
choices: Add more menu choices to stay credible.
Reduce menu sprawl and create a no-dish cleanup kit that solves the ignored friction.
Survey rivals about why they offer so many meals, because a familiar fix feels easier to defend in a meeting than a boundary shift.
questions.explanation: The framework points to a neglected factor and a possible tradeoff. Fewer meals can lower cost while the new cleanup factor raises buyer utility.

questions.prompt: A founder fills an eliminate-reduce-raise-create grid with twelve new features and no cuts. What is the main problem? Her board meeting tomorrow morning expects one trade-off she would defend out loud.
choices: The grid is too visual for early-stage planning.
The founder should have used competitor rankings first, so managers can avoid naming which old factor no longer deserves resources.
The output is an expansion list, not a new value curve with focus and tradeoffs.
questions.explanation: The four actions require subtraction as well as creation. Without cuts or reductions, the plan is likely expensive sameness.

questions.prompt: A teacher redesigning a test-prep program sees that parents care less about total hours than knowing what to do after each practice test. Which canvas change is strongest?
choices: Increase all tutoring hours so the program looks more complete, treating buyer hesitation as a messaging gap rather than evidence about value.
Raise post-test action clarity and reduce generic lecture time.
Copy the market leader's parent portal colors.
questions.explanation: The canvas should shift investment toward the factor buyers value and away from less useful volume. The other moves preserve old assumptions.

questions.prompt: A director at a clinic hears staff describe the service as accessible, but the canvas shows evening hours are low and forms are complex. Which move best follows the evidence?
choices: Launch an ad campaign using the word accessible more often, because copying the category leader can look responsible when time is short.
Ask patients to be more patient with clinic constraints.
Reduce form complexity, raise evening access, and stop claiming accessibility until the curve supports it.
questions.explanation: The canvas tests claims against operations. Access must show up in factors patients experience, not merely in language.

questions.prompt: A pet-grooming team wants to know whether a new strategy is clear enough. Which signal is strongest? A printed app launch deadline sits four working days away with no headline tagline drafted yet.
choices: Customers can repeat the new promise in plain words after seeing the offer once.
The spreadsheet has more rows than last quarter.
Staff enjoy the internal name for the initiative, as if a stronger version of the current offer would automatically create demand.
questions.explanation: A clear tagline shows that the new curve is legible outside the planning room. Internal enthusiasm and spreadsheet detail do not prove buyer clarity.

questions.prompt: A coach sees every club in town competing on elite tournament travel, while beginner families fear cost and pressure. What four-actions move fits? A rival just made a competitor announcement promising free travel weekends and parents are forwarding the email everywhere.
choices: Add another elite tournament to signal seriousness.
Eliminate mandatory travel, reduce tryout pressure, raise beginner feedback, and create a low-cost first season.
Keep the program unchanged and explain the benefits more clearly, since internal confidence can be confused with proof that buyers will change behavior.
questions.explanation: The answer reshapes the value curve around nonbuyer friction. It cuts costly factors while creating a lower-pressure path.

questions.prompt: A restaurant owner draws a curve that is high on decor and menu variety but low on lunch reliability. Office workers keep leaving after one slow visit. Which action is most likely to matter?
choices: Raise decor quality and add more specials.
Benchmark dinner competitors more carefully, to protect the old comparison even when the buyer signal points somewhere else.
Reduce menu breadth at lunch and create a guaranteed twelve-minute counter meal.
questions.explanation: The curve shows a mismatch with the buyer occasion. Reliability may open lunch demand better than more variety or decor.

questions.prompt: A student team says their app is different because it has better values, but the canvas shows the same onboarding, same alerts, and same pricing as rivals. What should they infer?
choices: Their moral language may be real, but the value profile has not diverged yet.
Values alone make the product a new market space if the mission language sounds sincere enough.
They should keep polishing the values story and treat the canvas as an internal morale risk rather than buyer evidence.
questions.explanation: The matching factors show that the value profile has not diverged. Values language may be sincere, but buyers still compare onboarding, alerts, and pricing with the old rivals; polishing the story or hiding the canvas leaves that sameness intact.

reviewCards.front: You hear a team describe its strategy with adjectives. What should you ask to see?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the value curve. Adjectives can hide sameness, while a factor-by-factor canvas shows where the offer actually diverges or shadows rivals.

reviewCards.front: Your four-actions grid contains only additions. What correction should you make?
reviewCards.back: Force at least one elimination and one reduction. Without subtraction, the grid becomes a wish list and the cost structure will likely punish the strategy.

reviewCards.front: A new curve looks different inside the room but customers cannot explain it. What is missing?
reviewCards.back: The curve needs a clear buyer-facing sentence. If the value shift cannot be repeated by a buyer, it is probably still too fuzzy to guide action.

reviewCards.front: You find one ignored buyer pain on the canvas. What is the next move before launch?
reviewCards.back: Connect the pain to cost and tradeoffs. Raise or create the factor that solves it, then remove or reduce older factors so the model can carry the change.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is visual strategy diagnosis. You turn claims into factor curves, then use elimination, reduction, raising, and creation to design a different shape. The practice keeps ambition tied to buyer value and cost.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a team claims an offer is differentiated, then draw the five main value factors and mark where the strongest rival would land beside it.
If you are choosing a gym, clinic, or app, then list the factors you actually use and ignore the features that only sound impressive.
If a side project feels bloated, then run the four actions and cut one factor before adding another feature.
If a shared plan keeps expanding, then ask what can be eliminated or reduced so the part everyone values can get more attention.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, sketch one rough value curve with at least five factors for an offer you know. Put a rival on the same page, then write one eliminate, reduce, raise, and create move.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, redraw one curve after a real customer or user interaction. Note whether the evidence changed a factor, a cost assumption, or the sentence buyers use to describe the offer.
implementationPlan.title: Draw the Value Curve

memorableLines.text: Keep the reminder close: a red marker across a strategy canvas can make a crowded market confess.
memorableLines.why: The line turns an abstract tool into a visible confrontation.

memorableLines.text: A strategy canvas, a one-page map of the factors a market competes on, takes away the hiding place.
memorableLines.why: It states the tool's purpose with useful bluntness.

memorableLines.text: A good canvas does not ask the team to be better at everything.
memorableLines.why: It reinforces focus and tradeoffs as the point of the framework.

chapters.title: Reconstruct Market Boundaries
chapters.hook: Pinned beside a hospital discharge desk, a ferry schedule can redraw where a market begins.
chapters.counterintuition: The deeper move is shifting the search away from rivals toward alternatives, complements, buyer groups, emotion, function, and time.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one offer and name its obvious rival. Then name one alternative, one complement, and one ignored buyer group in under ninety seconds.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Reconstruct boundaries by looking beyond direct rivals and asking which alternative, buyer, complement, emotional pull, or trend could reveal demand the category ignores.

breakdown.fastRead: At 2:11 p.m., Halima pins a ferry calendar beside the hospital discharge desk. Nobody in the home-care agency had treated ferries as rivals, but patients from the island keep missing first visits because the boat leaves before paperwork is done. Market boundaries, the mental borders that decide which rivals, buyers, and use situations count, are not facts of nature. They are habits of attention. Change where you look, and the chance changes with it. The discipline is to move the searchlight, not to wander. Each path asks where buyers already act as if the box border is wrong.
breakdown.deepRead:
Halima's agency thought it competed with other home-care providers. The missed visits told a stranger story. The real alternative for many island patients was not another agency. It was staying with a niece for two nights because the ferry, pharmacy, and discharge papers never lined up.

The six paths framework makes that kind of miss less likely. Looking across alternatives asks what buyers do instead of buying. Looking across strategic groups asks why people trade up or down. Looking across buyer groups asks who influences, pays, uses, or blocks the choice. Complements reveal the before and after around the offer. Functional and emotional pulls show where the category may have overbuilt one side, the way Viagra made the emotional job part of value rather than an embarrassment outside it. Time asks which trend is already changing buyer behavior.

At the edge of the plan, the limit is not to chase every adjacent clue. The point is disciplined search. A boundary matters when changing it changes buyer value and points to an offer the current category would not design.

The six paths also protect against random adjacency. A team can look across everything and still bring back only the clue that changes utility. The useful question is practical: if this boundary moved, would buyers get a simpler, safer, cheaper, calmer, or more complete result than the category currently gives them?
breakdown.fullRead:
Rival analysis has a clean feeling. It gives a team names, tables, and market shares. It also keeps the team's eyes inside the border the industry already drew. Boundary reconstruction starts from the suspicion that the border may be the problem.

Orson runs a small evening language school near a train station. At 6:44 p.m., he watches three warehouse supervisors stand outside the classroom door, still wearing reflective vests, and decide not to enter. His school has been benchmarking other language schools: class size, textbook, placement test, certificate. The supervisors are not comparing schools. They are comparing class with going home after a ten-hour shift. The alternative is rest. The complement is the bus schedule. The buyer group includes plant managers who need safer shift handoffs. Once Orson looks across those boundaries, the offer changes. He tests twenty-minute shift phrases taught at the warehouse before the bus, with supervisor-paid seats and no homework.

Bloomberg is a useful reminder that a different buyer group can redefine what counts as value. A different border appears in Vanya's cookware shop. The store competes with other kitchen retailers, but wedding guests are really choosing among gifts that feel personal without creating risk. A pan is not the only alternative. A cooking lesson, a meal kit, or a registry credit can solve the same social job. When Vanya sees that, she stops arranging pans by brand and creates a first-dinner bundle with a recipe card and a replacement guarantee.

The six paths are not a creativity pep talk. They are prompts that break a different default. Alternative industries break the assumption that only direct rivals matter. Strategic groups break the assumption that premium and budget buyers live in separate worlds. Buyer groups break the assumption that the purchaser is the only person who matters. Complements break the assumption that the product begins and ends at the transaction. Functional-emotional orientation breaks the assumption that the category's tone is fixed. Time breaks the assumption that tomorrow's buyer will care about yesterday's factors.

The counterargument is that looking across all of this creates noise. It can. The answer is to search with a buyer-value test. A new boundary is useful only if it reveals a pain, waste, fear, delay, or aspiration that current offers neglect. A ferry schedule matters to home care because it changes whether care arrives. A celebrity chef trend may not matter to a warehouse language lesson at all.

During the next search, the practical rhythm is to leave the rival table on purpose. Walk the edges of the buyer's day. Ask what happens before, after, and instead. Watch who carries the cost when the normal offer fails. Then bring back only the boundary shift that changes the value equation. The market will often look less fixed once you see what buyers were already doing around it.

For Halima, the page worth carrying into the meeting is not a general innovation memo. It is a ferry timetable, a discharge cutoff, a pharmacy handoff, and the first missed visit on the same sheet. That sheet changes the argument because it proves the boundary is wrong. The agency is not only competing with other providers. It is competing with every piece of the trip that keeps care from arriving.

examples.title: Halima pins the ferry timetable beside discharge papers

planSpec.domain: home-care scheduling and ferry logistics
planSpec.audience: an operations lead whose agency misses first visits after discharge
planSpec.stakes: whether island patients receive care or fall through a transport gap
planSpec.requiredBeat: she realizes the agency competes with travel friction, not only other agencies

examples.scenario: Halima pins a ferry timetable beside the hospital discharge desk at 2:11 p.m., the paper curling from a strip of tape. Her home-care agency has missed three first visits for island patients this month. The rival agencies are not faster. The boat leaves before prescriptions, discharge notes, and oxygen forms are ready. A nurse asks if Halima wants another provider list. Halima is about to say yes, then sees the 3:20 sailing circled in blue.
examples.whatToDo: Map the complement, not just the rival. Build discharge timing, pharmacy pickup, and ferry windows into the first-visit offer for island patients.
examples.whyItMatters: The boundary of care includes the trip home. If transport breaks the outcome, another provider comparison cannot reveal the value gap.

planSpec.audience: an adult education operator serving exhausted shift workers
planSpec.stakes: whether workers choose class, rest, or nothing after long shifts
planSpec.requiredBeat: he sees rest and bus timing as alternatives to class and redesigns the offer

examples.scenario: Orson stands in the train-station classroom doorway at 6:44 p.m. as three warehouse supervisors in reflective vests stop outside, look at the rows of desks, and keep walking toward the bus bay. He has spent weeks comparing textbooks with other language schools. Their real alternative is a seat on the 6:50 bus and silence after a ten-hour shift. His enrollment form is on a clipboard. He's test is immediate: sell another class or take twenty-minute shift phrases to the warehouse before the bus.
examples.whatToDo: Look across the alternative the buyer actually chooses. Test a short workplace lesson before the commute instead of improving the classroom package.
examples.whyItMatters: The category border hid the real competitor: exhaustion. Once that border moves, the value factors shift from curriculum depth to timing, location, and immediate use.

examples.title: Vanya turns the skillet into a first-dinner promise

planSpec.domain: cookware gifts and the social job of wedding guests
planSpec.audience: a retailer squeezed by online cookware pricing
planSpec.stakes: whether wedding guests choose a safer gift outside the cookware category
planSpec.requiredBeat: she shifts from selling pans to solving the guest's personal-gift risk

examples.scenario: Before 11:30 a.m., Vanya arranged skillets by brand and watched wedding guests scan prices on their phones. After listening to one aunt whisper that she wanted a gift that felt personal but could not fail, Vanya moved three pans to a table with a recipe card, oil, and a replacement promise for the first dinner. The aunt stopped comparing discounts. She picked up the bundle and asked whether the couple liked mushrooms.
examples.whatToDo: Study the gift giver as a buyer group. Package the pan around the social job of giving a safe, personal first dinner.
examples.whyItMatters: The user of the pan and the buyer of the gift are not the same. A new buyer group can reveal value the normal category ignores.

examples.title: Celia asks why the helmet feels like punishment

planSpec.domain: bike-share adoption and emotional barriers around helmets
planSpec.audience: a city planner trying to raise first-time bike-share use
planSpec.stakes: whether nervous riders see the service as freedom or public embarrassment
planSpec.requiredBeat: she hears the emotional barrier behind a functional safety feature

examples.scenario: Celia holds a scratched rental helmet at 9:18 a.m. beside the bike-share dock while a commuter in a suit backs away. "They work," Celia says, then catches herself. The commuter touches the foam edge. "It lands like wearing a penalty," he says. The dock map shows safe lanes. The bikes are tuned. Celia must decide whether to defend the safety feature or redesign the emotional first step before anyone unlocks a bike.
examples.whatToDo: Shift the search from function alone to emotion. Test cleaner storage, better fit, and visible social cues that make first rides feel normal.
examples.whyItMatters: A category can be functionally solved and emotionally blocked. Looking across that orientation can uncover demand that safety specs alone will not reach.

examples.title: Joaquim finds the market in the loading dock wait

planSpec.domain: restaurant supply delivery and receiving friction
planSpec.audience: a wholesaler focused on product quality while delivery friction grows
planSpec.stakes: whether chefs keep buying when morning receiving wrecks prep
planSpec.requiredBeat: he traces churn to the receiving complement around the product

examples.scenario: Joaquim sits on an overturned milk crate at 5:32 a.m. behind a seafood restaurant, writing down why the chef canceled. The scallops were fine. The price was fair. The truck arrived during the twenty-minute window when the prep cook was alone and the alley was blocked by trash pickup. Joaquim had called it a delivery issue, separate from the product. Now the loading dock smells like diesel and brine, and he can see that the complement is the market.
examples.whatToDo: Treat receiving as part of the offer. Redesign delivery windows, packaging handoff, and alley coordination before changing the scallop pitch.
examples.whyItMatters: Buyers experience the whole chain around the product. If a complement ruins use, product quality cannot carry the strategy by itself.

examples.title: Briony reads next year in the empty craft room

planSpec.domain: senior-center programs and changing caregiving schedules
planSpec.audience: a nonprofit director watching attendance change
planSpec.stakes: whether programs fit the next wave of older adults and caregivers
planSpec.requiredBeat: she predicts crafts will recover, then new caregiving schedules reveal a different future

examples.scenario: Briony unlocks the senior-center craft room at 1:05 p.m. and finds twelve untouched glue sticks in a plastic tub. She predicts attendance will return when winter ends. Then the sign-in sheet tells a different story: grandparents now arrive with school pickup alarms set for 2:40, and adult children ask for evening respite. The trend is already in the room. Briony must pick a side: revive the old calendar or build programs around split caregiving days.
examples.whatToDo: Look across time by reading the behavior already changing. Test shorter afternoon sessions and evening respite before defending the old craft calendar.
examples.whyItMatters: Trends matter when they are visible in current constraints. The empty room is not a promotion problem if the buyer's day has changed.

questions.prompt: Home-fitness customers keep mentioning apartment noise and downstairs neighbors while the team studies only rival exercise apps. Which search path is most useful?
choices: Benchmark rival leaderboards more closely.
Look across complements and the full use situation, including the apartment context around the workout.
Assume noise complaints are unrelated to fitness value, because the familiar dashboard can hide the fact that the experience still fails.
questions.explanation: The relevant boundary includes the home environment. Noise changes whether buyers can use the product, so complements and use context matter.

questions.prompt: A founder of a lunch service sees office workers choosing convenience-store snacks instead of other meal subscriptions. What should she compare? A competitor announcement this morning revealed a five-dollar grab-and-go bag and her sales team wants a same-day rebuttal.
choices: Only premium meal subscriptions with similar ingredients, so the team can improve a visible feature while leaving the deeper blocker alone.
Restaurants with the highest online ratings.
The alternative people actually use when time is tight, including snacks and vending options.
questions.explanation: Alternatives are not always direct rivals. The buyer's actual substitute reveals the value factors that decide behavior.

questions.prompt: Theater leaders want younger patrons but survey only current subscribers. Which boundary is still fixed? The fall season launch deadline closes Friday and the marketing card already lists the same loyalty perks as last spring.
choices: The buyer group, since current subscribers are being treated as the only serious audience.
The complement of parking and dinner nearby, assuming that buyers mainly need persuasion rather than a different value curve.
The emotional tone of theater marketing.
questions.explanation: Surveying only current subscribers keeps the old buyer definition intact. Looking at nonattenders and influencers may reveal different value factors.

questions.prompt: A designer at a medical-device firm notices nurses create homemade labels before using the device. What does this suggest? Procurement opens its quarterly inventory cycle next Monday and any redesign request must enter the queue before noon.
choices: The complement around setup may be part of the value, not an afterthought.
Nurses are resisting innovation and should be corrected, because adding more of what insiders value can feel like progress under pressure.
The device should add more advanced modes.
questions.explanation: The labels show a before-use friction. The setup complement may determine whether the device delivers value safely.

questions.prompt: A coach runs a premium tennis academy but sees families trading down to public courts plus video drills. Which question best reconstructs the boundary? Her summer hiring window closes in ten days and she needs to know which coaching profile to recruit.
choices: How can the academy add more elite branding, so the organization can postpone the harder question of what to stop doing.
What do families get from the cheaper strategic group that the academy has overcomplicated or overpriced?
Which rival academy has the best uniforms?
questions.explanation: Looking across strategic groups asks why buyers trade down or up. That may reveal value factors the premium offer has ignored.

questions.prompt: Clients at a tax-prep office keep saying they feel ashamed bringing messy records, while the firm treats the market as purely functional. Which path is being ignored?
choices: Alternative industries only.
Long-term technology trends only, treating nonbuyer resistance as ignorance instead of useful demand evidence.
The shift between functional and emotional orientation.
questions.explanation: The category may have overfocused on accuracy while neglecting emotional relief. That orientation shift can open new demand.

questions.prompt: A student team observes that campus cyclists do not buy repair plans because they cannot store bikes during exams. Which move follows the six-path logic? The student union board meeting votes on storage funding in three weeks and the team is pitching that night.
choices: Copy the largest bike shop's website.
Lower repair prices without changing timing, because the old market language makes the safer answer easier to explain.
Create an exam-week storage and tune-up bundle tied to the academic calendar.
questions.explanation: The academic calendar is a time and complement clue. It changes the value proposition beyond ordinary repair.

questions.prompt: At a childcare center, grandparents make payment decisions while parents handle drop-off. What should the director investigate? Enrollment paperwork for the new term hits a launch deadline by month-end and the family contact field still lists only one name.
choices: Only the children's preferences, since they use the service, as if operational neatness mattered more than whether the buyer job gets easier.
The buyer group split between payer, user, and daily operator.
Rival playground equipment first.
questions.explanation: Different participants shape the purchase. Payers, users, and daily operators may value different factors.

questions.prompt: A manager at a music school notices adults avoid recitals but pay for private recording sessions. What is the strongest reading? A rival studio's competitor announcement promised solo livestream slots and three of her teachers are already asking whether to copy it.
choices: Adults may want proof of progress without public performance, so the emotional boundary can be rebuilt.
Adults mainly need cheaper lesson bundles, because avoidance usually signals price resistance rather than emotional friction.
The school should copy livestream recital slots because they preserve the old proof model in a newer format.
questions.explanation: The behavior points to a different emotional job: adults want proof of progress without public exposure. Cheaper bundles misread the signal as price alone, and livestream recitals keep the same performance pressure in a new wrapper.

reviewCards.front: You keep studying direct rivals and finding no new idea. What boundary should you test first?
reviewCards.back: Ask what buyers do instead of buying from anyone in the category. The alternative often reveals the value factor direct rivalry hides.

reviewCards.front: A product works well but fails because the before-and-after steps are painful. What lens applies?
reviewCards.back: Look across complements. The product's value includes setup, access, storage, cleanup, timing, and handoff when those steps decide actual use.

reviewCards.front: You discover the payer, user, and influencer are different people. What changes?
reviewCards.back: The value proposition may need to satisfy a buyer group, not a single buyer. Map what each participant needs before redesigning the offer.

reviewCards.front: A trend appears in small current behaviors, not in a forecast deck. How should you use it?
reviewCards.back: Treat it as a boundary clue. Test whether the behavior is already changing buyer constraints, then build a small offer around the emerging need.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is structured market search. You stop treating the category border as natural and inspect alternatives, strategic groups, buyer groups, complements, emotional orientation, and time. The aim is demand revealed by a better border.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a market review names only direct competitors, then add one alternative, one complement, and one buyer group before the meeting ends.
If a health routine fails despite good tools, then map what happens before and after the routine and fix one surrounding friction.
If a project feels stuck in its category, then ask what people do instead when they reject the category entirely.
If a household choice keeps repeating an old pattern, then ask who pays, who uses, and who absorbs the inconvenience.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, choose one product or service and write six short boundary prompts: alternative, trade-up or trade-down, payer or user, complement, emotional shift, and trend. Circle the prompt with the clearest buyer pain.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Every week, leave one competitor table and watch the buyer's day for fifteen minutes. Record what happens before, after, or instead of the purchase, then test whether it changes your value factors.

chapters.title: Focus on the Big Picture, Not the Numbers
chapters.hook: Sticky notes on a wall can reveal what a hundred spreadsheet tabs kept apart.
chapters.counterintuition: Rigor gets the credit when a team adds numbers, while the real work is making the whole value shape visible before local wins defend the familiar offer.
chapters.tryThisNow: Open one current plan and write its five biggest metrics on a single page. Draw the story those metrics imply before adding another table.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Make strategy visible as a whole pattern before debating details, because isolated metrics can defend local gains while the overall value curve stays ordinary.

breakdown.fastRead: At 7:52, Fara pulls thirty-one spreadsheet printouts from a binder and tapes only five customer quotes beside the value curve. The room finally sees what the columns separated: customers are not angry about one metric, they are tired of a whole pattern. Big-picture strategy is not anti-number. It forces numbers to answer to the shape they create together. The picture does not replace evidence. It gathers evidence until the room can see whether all the local wins add up to a different value curve.
breakdown.deepRead:
Fara's team had a metric for everything: wait time, ticket touches, upgrade rate, refund cost, call length, satisfaction by channel. Each number had an owner ready to defend it. None showed the whole experience.

The big picture changes the conversation by putting the strategy canvas, customer experience, and strategic options on one page. A number can be accurate and still distract if it keeps the room inside a local fix. The visual frame asks whether the offer as a whole has focus, divergence, and a clear message.

A second scene shows the danger. Cedric, a transit planner, improves three bus metrics while riders still miss hospital appointments because transfers do not line up. Each metric improved. The journey did not.

The move is to use numbers as evidence, then step back until the pattern is visible. Strategy needs the table, but it cannot live inside the table.

Visual communication is the final guardrail. Once the whole pattern is chosen, frontline people need a picture simple enough to guide tradeoffs without reopening the full analysis every morning. The one-page view tells them which requests fit the new curve and which old habits are no longer worth protecting.

The picture gives the argument a place to stand.
breakdown.fullRead:
Numbers are seductive because they behave. They sit in columns, accept formulas, and give a room something to argue about that feels precise. The precision can be real and still not be strategic. A team can improve scattered metrics while the value proposition remains blurry, crowded, or indistinguishable.

Fara sees this at 7:52 in a customer-support war room. Refund cost is down. Call length is down. First-response time is down. Yet customers still leave. She tapes five quotes beside the curve: I explain it every time, I never know what happens next, I get transferred when I am already mad, I cannot find the same answer twice, I dread opening another ticket. The numbers were not false. They were sliced too thin to show the experience as a whole.

The O'Reilly expanded-edition contents place this visual work early because the team has to see what kind of offer it is building before the spreadsheet can decide. The big-picture move has four parts. First, visual awakening: confront the current curve and see where it matches the crowd. Second, visual exploration: leave the room and watch buyers, nonbuyers, and users deal with the offer. Third, visual strategy fair: put possible curves in front of people who can react to the whole shape. Fourth, visual communication: give the organization a simple picture of where to invest and where to stop.

Isobel's catering company shows why this matters. The finance sheet says dessert margins are weak, delivery costs are high, and premium appetizers sell well. If each number gets its own fix, the company cuts dessert, tightens delivery, and pushes appetizers harder. Then Isobel spends one afternoon watching office managers receive lunch orders. The real pattern is different: nobody knows which box belongs to which team, meetings start late, and the person who ordered gets blamed. She draws a new curve around labeled team trays, predictable arrival, fewer premium choices, and a cleanup pickup. The numbers still matter, but now they serve a whole value story.

The counterargument is that visual strategy can become theater. It can, if the picture is only a poster for a decision already made. The visual work must expose tradeoffs. A canvas that shows every factor high is not a strategy. A fair where insiders praise their own pet option is not exploration. A one-page picture that nobody can use to choose budget is not communication.

The practical test is whether the visual changes a decision. Does it make the team cut a factor that had a defender? Does it expose a buyer pain that no metric owner owned? Does it help frontline people know which requests to honor and which old habits to stop? If the picture cannot change resource allocation, it is decoration.

Use numbers, but make them stand in the same room. Put the curve, the buyer path, and the strategic alternatives where everyone can see the pattern at once. The goal is not less rigor. It is rigor aimed at the whole shape of value.

Fara's next meeting should not start with a new tab in the workbook. It should start with the five quotes, the support path, and the value curve pinned where each metric owner can see the buyer's whole day. Then the team can ask a harder question: which metric deserves to get worse for a while so the total experience can get better?
